Group Multiplication of Permutations

PermutationsAlgebraInvariants
Game: Two random shuffles, f and g, are multiplied in both orders, and each one is also "conjugated" by the other.
How to play: Press "Reset" for new shuffles. Tick "Show cycles" to write them as loops, and look at the loops of f⁻¹gf and g.
Look for the math

Permutations of 1, ..., N can be multiplied: do one and then the other. Written as fg, the left one is carried out first, so (fg)(k) = g(f(k)). The page shows fg, gf, and the two conjugates f-1gf and g-1fg.

Conjugates are the same loops, renamed

Write g as a product of cycles, say (a1 a2 ... ak). Then f-1gf has the cycle (f(a1) f(a2) ... f(ak)): every number is replaced by its image under f. To see it, start at f(ai): f-1 takes it to ai, g to ai+1, and f to f(ai+1). The test confirmed it for every pair of permutations of up to 5 numbers and for 20,000 random pairs up to 12 numbers.

Same shape, different permutation

So g and f-1gf have the same number of cycles of each length; they are conjugate. Since gf = f-1(fg)f, even fg and gf have the same shape of cycles, although as permutations they usually differ (the test found pairs with fg ≠ gf for every N from 3 to 5).

Writing a cycle

A cycle can start anywhere: (1 3 8 4), (3 8 4 1), (8 4 1 3) and (4 1 3 8) are one cycle. This page, like the applet, always starts with the smallest element.

Press Reset until f and g have different cycle shapes. Does f-1gf look like f or like g?
